Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024
A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.
This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.
In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.
At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.
There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.
On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.
"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.
"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."
Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.
"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).
Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.
In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".
Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.
Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.
In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.
Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.
According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.
Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

AI investing startup Supertake has an interesting premise: What if your “takes” on the market could make you money without you having to pick stocks yourself? The service lets people turn their ideas into real investment portfolios, using frontier AI models and trading agents.
Now, the company has raised $20 million in seed funding to grow its business. The round was led by venture firm Adjacent (Nico Wittenborn), with participation from Coinbase Ventures and Union Square Ventures (USV). Numerous angel investors also joined, including Nat Friedman , who’s currently head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs; Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch; renowned product manager Nikita Bier; investor Scott Belsky; and Nemil Dalal, a former Coinbase exec who is now a visiting partner at Y Combinator.
Michael Mignano originally incubated the startup at USV. He is the co-founder and former CEO of the podcasting platform Anchor, which Spotify acquired in 2019 for over $150 million. After leading Spotify’s podcasting business as “Head of Talk” for a few years, he joined the team at Lightspeed as a venture partner, betting on AI companies like Suno and Granola. He also co-founded Oboe, an AI education startup, and joined USV as a general partner in April.
“We really believed there was an opportunity to make investing more democratized…and give everyone and anyone the ability to invest in their own insights and beliefs and ideas,” Mignano said. While he will continue in his role as founder and executive chairman, he’s now brought in a team to run the company day to day.
The team includes co-founders Lincoln Murr (CEO) and John Peterson (CTO). Both joined from Coinbase, where, Mignano notes, they were the heads of AI product and engineering, leading launches like Coinbase advisor, Coinbase for agents, agentic wallets, and others.
The startup arrives as AI continues to make inroads into financial services, but allowing AI to take over people’s actual investments requires a new level of trust. Supertake is betting that people will ultimately be willing to take that leap, given recent improvements in frontier AI models.
Currently, Supertake works with Coinbase and Robinhood, and the company intends to expand to more brokerages over time. The idea is that you can explain, in broad, natural language, what you believe about how the world is going to change, and Supertake’s AI will iterate with you back and forth to turn that idea into a “take” that’s investable.
Under the hood, the startup is leveraging frontier AI technology and tools, combined with its own proprietary software that directs and limits what the AI can do.
Supertake’s users’ ideas are tracked on a leaderboard on the site, so others who agree can invest alongside them. For instance, there’s currently an idea on the leaderboard about looksmaxxing and longevity becoming more of a trend, where the portfolio includes certain pharma and cosmetic companies that could potentially benefit.
For now, these portfolios consist of stock picks, but the team wants to expand the service over time to handle other types of transactions, like shorts, derivatives, perpetuals, long exposure, or even prediction markets — the latter handled through partnerships with companies in that space.
Despite these “takes” seeming like bets on what could happen next in a given market, Murr stresses that this doesn’t make Supertake itself a prediction market.
“We think it’s a novel and very much improved way to create what was previously considered the robo-advisor experience,” he says. “When that came out, it had this amazing vision and direction of allowing people to have digital asset management. We think now is actually the time for that, with AI agents being so widely proliferated.”
“I don’t think this is necessarily a prediction market by any means. The idea of natural language translation into an underlying set of assets feels different in that regard,” he says.
Still, the startup could wade into short-term predictions if a user’s take involves something they believe could happen in the near future, like who might win an election.
“We’re primarily focused on the longer, medium-term holdings today. But that being said, we don’t want to preclude people from building out very hyper short-term strategies that might exist,” Murr adds.
To address people’s concerns over AI managing their money, Supertake’s team says it’s implementing certain guardrails and spend limits. For instance, the AI has no ability to deposit or withdraw funds on a user’s behalf without their explicit consent. There are also drift limits in place so the portfolio stays balanced, plus allow and deny lists (meaning which assets the AI may and may not trade), real-time monitoring for anomalous activity, tools to set trade size limits, and a restriction that keeps agents from seeing the user’s brokerage credentials.
“We view it as somewhat analogous to self-driving cars, actually, where there is a spectrum here of both trust and technological innovations that are happening,” says Murr. “Where a few years ago you may not feel comfortable getting in a car that has lane assist, but today you get in a Waymo, and it’s like nothing. And we think that there’s a very similar progression happening with the agentic finance space, and we’re far further along in the technological spectrum than people think.”
Access to Supertake is still behind a waitlist while in beta, but the founders said they’ve put their money where their mouths are. Murr and Peterson are letting it manage “tens of thousands” and “thousands” of dollars, respectively.
Mignano, meanwhile, says he has Supertake managing “hundreds of thousands” of dollars.
With the new funding, which follows a $2 million pre-seed round, Supertake aims to expand its team in areas like engineering, design, growth marketing, and others. Mignano and Murr are in New York, while Peterson is in the Austin area but commutes to New York at times. The team says it hopes to figure out a hybrid work model as it grows.

Iran flogged pop singer Parastoo Ahmadi and four members of her concert team on Monday following a December 2024 performance near Qom in which she sang without a hijab, her lawyer said.
Lawyer Mostafa Nili told Emtedad news channel that the Qom prosecutor's office enforcement team carried out the sentence against Ahmadi in the early hours of Monday.
The flogging sentences against band members Sohail Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri and Amirali Pirnia, and concert organiser Mohsen Lashkari, were carried out on the same day, Nili said.
A criminal court in Qom province had sentenced nine members of the concert team to 74 lashes each, a two-year ban on leaving the country and a two-year ban on artistic activity.
The judiciary also sealed off the Deyr Gachin Caravanserai, the historic venue where the concert took place.
Ahmadi performed at the caravanserai near the historic city of Qom on the evening of 11 December 2024 without hijab. No audience was present.
The concert was broadcast live on YouTube and drew around 3 million views in the days that followed.
Ahmadi described the performance as a "hypothetical concert." Writing on her YouTube channel, she said, "I want to sing for the people I love. This is a right that I could not give up, that is, singing for the land that I love passionately."
The criminal court of Qom charged the group with "offending public decency by producing and disseminating vulgar and immoral content online."
Amnesty International called in June for the sentences to be quashed, saying flogging was "a cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment" that violated the absolute prohibition on torture and other ill-treatment.
The organisation called on Tehran to abolish compulsory veiling and corporal punishment and to end the criminalisation of freedom of expression.
Under Islamic Republic law, women are banned from singing in public in spaces where men are present.
Although criminal law does not explicitly criminalise women's singing as such, female performers typically face charges of encouraging corruption and prostitution, failing to observe hijab, or offending public decency.
Authorities have used the charge in recent years to close many Instagram pages belonging to Iranian female singers. Appearing in public without hijab is punishable by between 10 days and two months in prison, up to 74 lashes or a fine.
The sentences against Ahmadi and her collaborators stand in contrast to scenes from pro-government rallies held during the US and Israeli military strikes on Iran earlier in 2026, when images circulated widely showing women at the gatherings without mandatory hijab.
A performance by Lebanese singer Julia Boutros was also broadcast at a pro-government gathering in Tehran, where Boutros also did not wear hijab.
Earlier, during the Woman, Life, Freedom protest movement in 2022, Ahmadi had performed the protest song "Az khun-e javanan-e vatan" or "From the blood of the nation's youths".
After it was widely shared on social media, her home was searched by security forces and she was ordered to report to the security prosecutor's office in Tehran.
The Woman, Life, Freedom movement emerged in Iran in September 2022 following the death of Mahsa Amini, 21, in the custody of Tehran's morality police. Amini had been detained over alleged issues with her hijab.
Human rights organisations say the subsequent crackdown left more than 500 people dead.

Watch: Democrat who unseated 21-year Republican incumbent says party needs to 'bring change'
The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.
The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.
Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.
Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.
"I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change. They voted for change," Hubbard told the BBC News Channel after his victory. He pledged to work alongside his fellow lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable.
Earlier, he wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".
Hubbard added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."
Foxx, meanwhile, said in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."
Virginia Foxx spent a decade in the North Carolina Senate before representing the state in the House of Representatives
Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx two years ago by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.
Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.
Trump himself - as well as Vice President JD Vance - have suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses.
Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.
The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.
Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.
However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux.
I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^)
Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional.
This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.
We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!
The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that.
If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol.
Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

The Democratic Party is debating how best to use its large margin of victory in the US midterm elections.
The Democratic Party has continued to expand its already sizeable majorities in the United States Congress as counting concludes in the final races of the 2026 midterm elections .
As of Monday, the Democrats hold a 258-seat majority in the 435-member House of Representatives. Four races remain uncalled.
All the races have been decided, meanwhile, for the Senate, where Democrats gained a 56-seat majority out of 100 total seats.
Flipping both chambers gives the party a strong hand to shape legislation during the last two years of Trump’s term in office.
How might the Democrats approach their role in government once the new Congress is sworn in on January 3? Find out in this quick explainer.
The midterm results give Democrats their largest House majority since 1992 and their largest Senate majority in more than a decade. Republicans, meanwhile, saw their tally in the House drop to 173 seats, their lowest figure in years.
The vote also served as a firm rebuke of Trump’s second term as president, with voters venting their frustration over cost-of-living issues, the US-Israel war on Iran , aggressive immigration raids and corruption.
Democratic victories also extended well beyond traditional left-wing strongholds, with candidates racking up wins in Republican-led states such as Texas , Mississippi and South Carolina.
Four House seats have yet to be called: one in Minnesota, one in Tennessee, and two in Louisiana that will be settled by a run-off on December 12.
Those races could see the Democrats further expand their majority in the House. The final count is now a question of just how large the party’s majority will be.
Democrats have long pledged to use any congressional majorities they win as a check on Trump’s agenda.
But the scale of their success in the 2026 midterms has prompted discussion about embracing a more ambitious legislative agenda.
In the House of Representatives, Democrats have outlined a 100-day agenda that includes potentially reversing tax cuts that largely benefit wealthy earners and restoring healthcare subsidies that expired under Trump.
Lawmakers have also said that they will act to end the war on Iran, although divisions remain within the party over how to rein in Trump’s military actions. Under the US Constitution, Congress alone can authorise military operations.
Progressives have accused the party’s moderate wing of playing down expectations of firm steps to end the war, including cutting off funding.
Democrats have also pledged to use their newfound position to exercise oversight over the executive branch by launching probes and issuing subpoenas.
On Monday, for example, House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said that a Democrat-led Congress would conduct a “swift, thorough, and wide-ranging” investigation into the actions of the chip manufacturer Nvidia.
He also said it would delve into the “corrupt abuse of power” by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
In the Senate, Democrats have also threatened to block Trump’s nominees for high-level government positions, which require the chamber’s confirmation.
While Democrats will hold substantial majorities in both chambers of Congress, Trump will retain the power to veto legislation.
Some lawmakers, however, have tried to persuade the president that he could benefit from working with Democrats after his party’s stark defeat in the midterms.
Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed , for example, has shared a series of tongue-in-cheek social media posts suggesting that a universal healthcare programme — a long-term progressive goal — could be named after the president in a bid to win his support.
“Donald, this is on the table,” El-Sayed said in a social media post showing a card for a hypothetical health insurance programme titled “Trumpcare”. “Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”
There is little evidence, however, to suggest that Trump is planning a political pivot after the midterms.
Within a week of the vote, for instance, Trump named Stephen Miller — one of the architects of his hardline policies on immigration — as White House chief of staff.
The staffing shake-up was seen as a doubling-down on right-wing policy priorities.
While Trump has, at times, suggested that he could cooperate with Democratic lawmakers, he has also promised to use his veto power aggressively.
He has also taken to social media to disparage Chuck Schumer , who is currently seeking to become the next Senate majority leader, a position he previously held from 2021 to 2025.
“It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Sunday.
“He failed badly as ‘Leader’ once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again.”
Trump’s White House has also threatened to take action if Democrats aggressively use their oversight powers in Congress.
“Members of the new Congress have evinced a clear intent to transgress” the constitutional limits of their power, White House counsel Will Scharf wrote in a letter on November 9, gesturing to the prospect of congressional investigations.

The European Commission has presented its 22nd package of sanctions on Russia in a bid to “keep pressure” on Russia and “strike harder” at its ability to fund the war in Ukraine ( 16 :03 ).
The package includes measures on Russian banking ( 16:04 ), energy ( 16:05 ) and sports ( 16:06 , 16:07 , 16:09 ).
The latest announcement shows that sanctions hawks are in the ascendancy as the EU grows frustrated with Russia’s continiuing strikes on Ukraine ( 16:46 ).
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said it was “a mistake” that the Nato summit in Bucharest in 2008 did not accept the proposal to accept Ukraine as a Nato member , as he backed Emmanuel Macron’s call to revisit the idea of allowing Ukraine to join the alliance ( 15:53 ).
Merz and Nato’s Rutte both condemned the latest security incidents in Estonia, Finland and Poland ( 15:41 , 15:45 , 15:46 ).
“We are all targeted … and we are in this for the long term,” Rutte warned, as he called for increased defence spending ( 11:47 ).

After a period of doubts about the EU’s ability to introduce meaningful new sanctions on Russia , the European Commission is again attempting to increase the pressure.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen , has revived a proposal to ban Russian soldiers from entering EU territory, as part of a package of restrictions on Russian banking ( 16:04 ), energy ( 16:05 ) and sports ( 16:06 , 16:07 , 16:09 ) announced today, the 22nd round of sanctions against the Kremlin’s war machine.
A few months ago it was not certain there would be any substance to a 22nd package.
During painful negotiations over the 21st package in July, one existing sanction (on the transfer of liquified natural gas) was diluted and EU member states delayed a plan to ban ex-combatants from entering the bloc, amid opposition from France and Italy, two countries that have handed out large numbers of tourist visas. Then September saw two oligarchs removed from the EU sanctions list.
Von der Leyen concluded in the same month that the EU should focus on closing loopholes. “What is needed is not necessarily new sanctions, but above all the enforcement of existing sanctions,” she said in her state of the union speech.
But since then, Russia has intensified its bombardment of Ukraine exacting a terrible price in lives. And there have been more hostile acts in the EU blamed on Russia, such as the attempted assassination of a US-Ukranian rapper in Denmark attributed to Russian intelligence services, the thwarted Leipzig airport drone attack, and a spate of deadly drone strikes in the Black Sea.
The latest announcement shows that sanctions hawks are in the ascendancy, such as Estonia , which has championed the cause of banning Russian ex-combatants from EU territory, as well as prohibiting Russians from competing in sports events under their national flag.
This does not mean the latest package is guaranteed to pass intact – sanctions still have to be agreed by 27 member states unanimously – but the argument that the EU does not need new measures is less and less convincing for top policymakers in Brussels. The calculus has changed.
Meanwhile, Finland has summoned the Russian ambassador to condemn recent attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine and incidents in Europe.
“Finland has summoned the Russian Ambassador. We strongly condemn Russia’s illegal war of aggression and its escalating strikes against civilian targets in Ukraine. We stand in solidarity with Denmark, Poland and our other European partners.
Russia’s dangerous and reckless actions in Europe are unacceptable. A Russian helicopter is also suspected of violating Finnish airspace on Saturday 21 November.
Ukraine has the right to defend itself against Russia’s illegal aggression. Russia must end its war of aggression against Ukraine.”
The EU’s accompanying release says that the ban on Russian sportspeople means that “ Member States notably should consider refusing Schengen visas to Russian athletes competing in sporting events where Russian national symbols such as the flag, anthem, or uniforms are used.”
“The guidelines call as well for specific attention to be given to individual artists participating in cultural events , who are sponsored by the Russian authorities and who can use their visibility in favour of Russia’s war of aggression.”
The EU will also introduce “bans on Russian teams and athletes competing under the Russian flag,” von der Leyen says.
We will also restrict financial flows from Russian sponsors to European based sports and cultural associations, and we will introduce restrictions on Russians holding posts in governing bodies of European based sports federations.
“Our position is clear. We’re giving Ukraine the strength to secure a peace. And Russia, every reason to choose it.”
Von der Leyen also says the EU will “prohibit Europeans from continuing to occupy posts in the governing bodies of companies in Russia .”
“There cannot be business as usual in our economic relations with Russia.”
Von der Leyen says the EU will also “propose a visa ban for Russian ex-combatants.”
“We have recently seen an escalation in non-conventional kinetic activities of Russian operatives in Europe. And this ban is a part of our response.
Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries. Therefore, entry into the European Union will be off limits.”
On energy, the EU is “expanding the energy services ban so that no European company can help Russia build, operate or repair its energy infrastructures and notably its refineries,” von der Leyen said.
“For the first time, this ban also covers electricity services on the Russian shadow fleet. We are listing over 70 more ships and we are proposing to ban all tanker vessels, which are, in short, in Russia.”
On financial services, the new measures “extend the transaction ban to some 60 Russian banks,” which will be removed from the Swift system.
“And we’re cracking down on the crypto and payment networks. We will focus on Russia, but also include third countries that help Russia to evade our sanctions.
This is a major focus of our new package and an important area where we want to align efforts with international partners, and this is the reason why we have also launched a crypto sanctions taskforce to support this work.”
“The aim is to keep pressure on Russia to end their war of aggression in Ukraine, and we will continue to propose new sanctions until Russia shows genuine intent for lasting peace in Ukraine.
With this package, we are increasing the pressure in three ways:
We’re striking harder at Russia’s way to finance its war by targeting its banks and crypto platforms.
We’re shutting the door to its participation to European sports and cultural events. We’re tightening our visa rules, sports and cultural events. We’re tightening our visa rules, and we’re doubling down on enforcement.”
Meanwhile in Brussels, the European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen is just announcing the EU’s 22nd package of sanctions against Russia .
Meanwhile, Merz has gone as far as to say that it was a “mistake” that the Nato summit in Bucharest in 2008 did not accept the proposal to accept Ukraine as a Nato member.
“If Ukraine had become a member of Nato [then], this war would have possibly probably been prevented,” he said.

A few people have turned up at Brussels airport where no flights are leaving
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well as at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Underground services have also been halted in capital Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march.
The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.
No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers.
"In total, 404 flights today cannot be operated, which has an impact on more than 50,000 passengers," Brussels Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said.
Reuters news agency spoke to Florence Faure, a French passenger who had arrived in Brussels from China's capital, Beijing, only to find that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport had been cancelled.
"Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn't even collect it," she said.
A similar situation has affected Charleroi, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure or arrival.
One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she had received no warning and only discovered there were no flights when she arrived at the airport.
Philippe Naime, a teacher, was one of the tens of thousands taking part in the protest march in Brussels.
"Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves. But people do not have the means to do that," he told Reuters.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.
Large numbers of people have descended on Brussels for a protest march
One of its members, the socialist Vooruit, has been refusing to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants to raise taxes on the rich and for there to be fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse.
"While expressing regret over the lack of significant progress, the king encouraged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible," the royal palace said in a statement.
The leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
Bert Engelaar, head of the union, called for "a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes".
"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," he added, praising the Vooruit party.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

The European Commission has proposed new sanctions against Russia targeting its banks, crypto platforms, and participation in sporting events.
Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen introduced the 22nd package of sanctions on Monday, which includes a ban on Russian teams and individual athletes competing under the country’s flag at events in the European Union.
“We are striking harder at Russia’s ways to finance its war, by targeting its banks and crypto platforms,” von der Leyen wrote in a post on X, adding that the EU will be “shutting the door to its participation in European sports and cultural events”.
Von der Leyen said 60 banks will be removed from the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) messaging system used for international payments under the new proposals, which are intended to maintain economic pressure on Russia, almost five years into its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
She announced the creation of a crypto sanctions task force seeking to curb countries helping Russia to evade sanctions.
The commission also proposed a ban on visas for Russians who had fought in the war in Ukraine.
“Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries,” von der Leyen said.
The plan also put forward restrictions on financial flows from Russian sponsors to sports and cultural associations based in the EU. Russian nationals would also no longer be allowed to hold leadership positions on the governing bodies of sports federations.
“Sports events cannot be a forum for propaganda activities,” said von der Leyen.
The proposed package must be endorsed by all 27 EU member countries before going into force and comes just over a month after the bloc posted the largest listing of sanctions against Russia, targeting about 1,600 Russian officials and companies linked to its arms industry.
The EU has already slapped sanctions on more than 4,200 people and entities, including Russian President Vladimir Putin and several energy companies.

Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.
The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi , co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes , has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.
Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.
The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.
And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.
It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".
Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.
Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.
If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?
As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.
On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders , just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.
This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.
It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.
But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much – but not all – of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.
Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missile
Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.
In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.
The three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.
There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.
Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.
It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.
This autumn, Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.
There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

14 from Europe, Africa and Oceania have acknowledged a landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, calling on the country to comply with its obligations under international law. The United Kingdom separately announced sanctions against five senior Myanmar military figures and said it would formally recognise the genocide.
The UK and 13 other countries on Monday "acknowledged" the top UN court's ruling that Myanmar perpetrated genocide against its Rohingya minority as London announced new sanctions.
The foreign ministers of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, The Gambia and the United Kingdom said Myanmar had "violated its obligations under the Genocide Convention".
"We underscore that the Court's judgment is binding upon Myanmar and call on Myanmar to comply fully with its obligations under international law, including the Court's decision," they said in a joint statement.
The UK separately said it "formally recognises" genocide against the Rohingya and announced sanctions on five senior military figures.
"The horrific violence and persecution inflicted on the Rohingya cannot go unanswered," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said.
The sanctions include asset freezes and travel bans, a Foreign Office statement said, adding that London "also intends to introduce legislation targeting the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar".
"The UK is providing an additional £5m in new funding to support Rohingya and other communities with essential lifesaving and life-affirming services to approximately 350,000 people who need it most in Rakhine state, where humanitarian need is most acute," the statement added.
It said a further £3 million would "go towards strengthening accountability and justice for survivors of human rights abuses across Myanmar."
On November 19 in a historic verdict, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 crackdown in the western Rakhine state.
The ruling was the first time in the ICJ's 80-year history that it has determined that a state committed genocide.
Myanmar's government called the ruling unfair and a "great disappointment".
Shortly after the verdict, Britain announced it would expel Myanmar's defence attache.

Watch: Carney and Trump impersonators take stage with real Mark Carney
Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.
The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.
Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney.
"We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.
Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress.
"I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala.
He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."
There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians.
"I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.
Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator."
Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration.
The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster , external and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's , external support for Trump.
They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media. , external
Critch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.
In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel.
"Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

Watch: Coughing, confusion and boos as Co-op Live concert cancelled
Police are investigating after thousands of people were evacuated from a concert in Manchester following an "unknown substance" being released into the crowd.
It happened towards the end of US rapper Don Toliver's show at the Co-op Live arena at about 22:00 GMT on Sunday, with fans describing a "horrible smell" and people "screaming" and "coughing up blood".
One woman was taken to hospital for treatment, while 88 other people were assessed by paramedics for "eye and respiratory symptoms".
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said detectives were trying to establish what the substance was and where it came from and further testing was taking place on items found at the venue.
A major incident was declared after reports of people suffering from the effects of an unknown substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.
The force said no arrests had yet been made and detectives were investigating "whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident".
GMP said 88 people underwent "dry decontamination at the scene" and were accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed.
Some 12,000 people were evacuated and one fan told of "distressing scenes" with people "choking" and coughing as they left the venue.
Some fans have complained about security and a lack of searches going in to the concert.
A group of friends from Scunthorpe was standing in the mosh pit when the substance was released and said they "heard a pop" and "everyone coughing" and running away.
Molly, 19, said: "People not breathing, gagging, gasping for air. It was quite traumatic.
"People being wheeled out in wheelchairs covered in tinfoil, and no-one in the venue knew what was going on."
Kyan, 22, said: "When you breathed it in you tasted something weird. It didn't sit right - constant coughing, it sent a sting into your eyes."
The friends were later taken to the Etihad Stadium for the decontamination process.
Jack, 21, said some people had "pink liquid" on them and they were taken off to be tested.
"We were told to take off our clothes, and put on hazmat suits, slippers and a mask and taken to the Etihad to be observed," he said.
Charlie, 20, said he found the process a bit "invasive" and "confusing".
The friends said they were still suffering from symptoms, with a headache, chest pains and "really sore throat".
'People were screaming in pain' during Co-op Live evacuation
Molly, 19, Kyan 22, Charlie, 20, and Jack, 21, say they were taken to the decontamination process
Joey Howe was at the gig and recalled the incident happening 30 or 40 minutes in.
The 22-year-old told BBC Radio Manchester : "I saw a lot of people streaming out and you go into this panic mode and you see a lot of people running out of the venue.
Joey Howe says he wondered if it was "part of the show" until the smell hit
He said it was like "time stopped in motion" when "there was nothing going on".
"We then decided to go out. People were coming through in wheelchairs choking - it was really distressing," Howe said.
"We then decided to leave the venue. It was just really distressing scenes and not something you want to see."
Howe also claimed security was "poor" and "very relaxed" with "people walking straight in".
Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they had fled the venue.
The 23-year-old told the BBC that she went to the exit and saw lads on the bridge which leads into Medlock Square "asking for help" but there were only two stewards outside.
She said she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".
Concertgoers headed home after the performance was stopped by the incident
Malachi Clarke claimed security was "not good at all" at the venue.
The 19-year-old said: "They weren't checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine."
"Then we were told by a security guard it was chemical-related.
"After an hour or so of the gig being stopped, we were finally told to evacuate the venue."
Emergency services attended the Co-op Live arena in Manchester after a substance was let off in the crowd
Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".
It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".
Harper, who was at the concert, told BBC Radio 5Live : "I was right on the opposite side and I was seeing people cough up blood - I mean, that's when it was really scary for some of us, especially my girlfriend and I.
"I was in shock because I had no idea what was going on because it just stopped and all the lights came on.
"I saw people getting wheelchairs out...I was fearful it was something even worse."
Forensic officers are at the arena carrying out investigations
Fans at the rapper's other gigs have claimed similar incidents have taken place earlier on his tour.
They reported that a spray or gas was released into the crowd in Zurich and Paris.
Entrances to Co-op Live remain cordoned off, with police officers and security stewards manning the perimeter which is taped off.
Crime scene investigators in white protective overalls have been moving in and out of the building, as work continues to establish the nature of the substance that caused the evacuation.
The force said it was "an isolated incident" and there was "no wider threat to the public".
Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "Enquiries remain ongoing to establish the nature of the substance, where it came from and any associated risk."
He added that more than 12,000 people had been "safely escorted" from the arena and thanked concertgoers for their "patience".
Harding urged anyone who left the event and had since become unwell to attend their local hospital.
Don Toliver recently received five nominations for the 2027 Grammy awards (file photo)
The ambulance service added: "Decontamination was carried out as a precaution and one patient was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment."
It said several crews attended, including the Hazardous Area Response Team.
Anyone who has since "noticed side-effects or become ill" is urged to seek medical advice.
There was a large police presence at the venue on Monday morning
In a statement, Co-op Live said venue bosses were working closely with police to identify the cause of the incident.
"Our priority remains the safety and security of all visitors to Co-op Live, and we will provide more information once we have an update from GMP," the statement said.
Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig said the major incident had now ended and she thanked emergency services and venue staff for their "professionalism".
"Enquiries into the cause of the incident are ongoing so those affected can get the answers they deserve," she added.
Toliver, whose real name is Caleb Zackery Toliver, was performing in Manchester as part of his Nitrous tour.
The 32-year-old musician has received five nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards, including for Best New Artist.

Carney watches on as comedian lampoons US leader and his interest in men’s backsides at correspondents’ event Ottawa
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a Donald Trump impersonator who mocked the US president to raucous laughter from a crowd of politicians and journalists at a parliamentary press gallery dinner on Saturday.
With coiffed hair and an ill-fitting suit, comedian Mark Critch – who portrays the president on the sketch show This Hour Has 22 Minutes – danced on to the stage and lampooned the trade war Trump started as well as the president’s threats to annex Canada .
“We’re going to have a great deal,” Critch said, channeling Trump’s distinct mannerisms. “There’s only one thing standing in the way: me, because I’m crazy.”
The fake Trump continued that he was “so popular we just had a big, blue wave”, a reference to the Democratic rout of Republicans in this month’s US midterm elections.
He also mocked Trump’s frequent mentions of other men’s physiques, saying of the comedian Mark McKinney, who was portraying Carney, that he had “a great ass – doesn’t he? What a beautiful ass, he’s got such an incredible ass.”
He earned the most laughter of his short appearance for saying of Carney: “I don’t call him the governor to his face, because I’m a coward”. The real Trump has frequently attempted to insult Canada’s leaders by calling them governor, not prime minister, suggesting Canada is a US state.
The annual dinner, attended by media, political leaders and lobbyists, is often defined by carefully written jokes by the staff of party leaders.
Throughout his own 16-minute set, Carney poked fun at his political rivals, the media and the US president.
At one point, he remarked: “Damn, this is a tough room, and I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator.”
Clips of the dinner, including the crowd laughing at the president, have circulated widely on US media.
The newly appointed governor general, Louise Arbour, also gave a speech, including a nod to the prime minister’s decision to travel extensively around the globe.
“Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney ? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be,” she said.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, also used the evening to poke fun at his own reputation.
“Some say that Mark has a controlling leadership style. There’s been reports that he yells and micromanages his staff. He acts like a miserable prick to journalists,” he said. “And when I hear things like that, I say once again, he’s stealing all my ideas.”
He attracted a stunned silence, however, for alluding to Justin Trudeau’s relationship with Katy Perry, saying, “Trudeau is running around the world doing to a faded pop princess what he did to Canada” while prime minister, a remark that was widely criticised as demeaning to the pop star.
The New Democratic party leader, Avi Lewis, who has not yet won a seat in parliament, took a shot at Carney’s early exit from the event, as well his own party’s dismal standings. “I do not have a seat in the House of Commons, but when I am given one at dinner, I stay there all night long,” he said.

Galatasaray , UEFA Şampiyonlar Ligi 'nin 5. haftasında 24 Kasım Salı günü saat 20.45'te RAMS Park'ta Aston Villa'yı konuk edecek. Karşılaşma TRT 1'den canlı yayınlanacak. Milli maç arasından beri süren çim yenileme çalışmalarının ardından zeminin toparlandığı görülüyor. Ancak bazı bölümlerde kumların belirgin şekilde seçilmesi, maçın sorunsuz oynanıp oynanamayacağı sorusunu gündeme getirdi.
Milli maç arasından beri aralıksız süren çalışmalar sonucunda RAMS Park zemininin toparlandığı görülüyor. Buna rağmen bazı bölümlerde kumların zemin üzerinde belirgin şekilde seçilmesi dikkat çekti. Kumların zemine tam anlamıyla oturmaması, maçın oynanıp oynanamayacağı konusunda soru işaretleri yarattı. Sarı-kırmızılılar, stadyum zeminindeki sorun nedeniyle Süper Lig'in 12. haftasında Samsunspor'u Başakşehir Fatih Terim Stadyumu'nda ağırlamıştı.
UEFA, ev sahibi kulübün saha zeminini mümkün olan en iyi oyun koşullarında tutmasını zorunlu kılıyor. Kulüp, zeminin futbol oynamaya elverişli olması için gerekli tüm makul önlemleri almak zorunda. UEFA müsabaka öncesinde saha zeminini denetleyebiliyor ve hava koşulları gerektiriyorsa saha ısıtma ya da koruma sistemlerinin kullanılması isteniyor. UEFA Stadyum Talimatı'nın 5.01 maddesinde şu ifade yer alıyor:
'Oyun alanı düzgün ve düz olmalı, IFAB Oyun Kuralları'na uygun olmalıdır.'
Bu yüzden ciddi çukurlar, tehlikeli bozulmalar ya da futbolcuların güvenliğini tehdit eden sorunlar, UEFA'nın saha standartlarına aykırılık sayılabiliyor.
UEFA kurallarına göre bozuk zeminde de Şampiyonlar Ligi maçı oynanabiliyor. Çimlerin seyrek ya da sararmış olması tek başına otomatik erteleme nedeni sayılmıyor. Hakem sahada derin çukur , buzlanma ya da don, aşırı çamurlaşma ve drenaj yetersizliğinden kaynaklanan su birikintisi olup olmadığına bakıyor. Top normal şekilde sekmiyor ya da yuvarlanmıyorsa veya zemin futbolcular için ciddi sakatlık riski taşıyorsa maç ertelenebiliyor ya da tatil edilebiliyor. Aşırı yağış yüzünden saha oynanamaz hale gelirse de aynı yol izleniyor.
Zemin maç gününe kadar standartlara getirilemezse UEFA ev sahibi kulübe uyarı veriyor. Para cezası kesmesi ya da maçın standartlara uygun başka bir stadyuma, yani tarafsız sahaya alınmasına hükmetmesi de mümkün. UEFA'nın 26. maddesi, zemin müsabakaya uygun değilse maçın saatinin, tarihinin ya da stadyumunun değiştirilmesine izin veriyor. Maç öncesinde bu kararı UEFA yönetimi veriyor. Maç başladıktan sonra zemin elverişsiz hale gelirse hakem, UEFA delegesiyle ve mümkünse UEFA yönetimiyle görüşüp karşılaşmayı durdurabiliyor. Oynanamayacağına karar verilen maç kural olarak ertesi gün oynanıyor, bu mümkün olmazsa yeni tarihi UEFA belirliyor.

US rapper Don Toliver has postponed two shows in London this week, after his concert in Manchester on Sunday was evacuated when an "unknown substance" was released into the crowd.
Toliver was due to play The O2 on Monday and Wembley Arena on Tuesday, but Live Nation said his "stage and production equipment remains in Manchester and cannot be moved in time".
One person was taken to hospital and 89 people showed "symptoms believed to be linked to the exposure" after Sunday's Co-op Live arena show, police said.
Fans described "distressing scenes" with people "choking", "screaming" and "coughing up blood" because of the effects of a substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.
Watch: Coughs, confusion and boos as Co-op Live concert cancelled
The Wembley show has been rescheduled to 14 December, while Monday night's O2 gig has been moved to 15 December.
"I'm very sad to sit here and say I have to reschedule The O2 London show to December 15th due to (the) unfortunate incident last night," Don Toliver wrote on Instagram.
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) declared a major incident on Sunday and said 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena.
One woman was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment and treatment after the incident, which happened at about 22:00 GMT, the force said.
A further 88 people "underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were subsequently accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed", according to GMP.
Leon Douzi said he was right next to where the substance was released, and described someone holding a can and "this gas coming out".
"It just hit me in the throat," he said, adding that it felt like "burning".
There was "a bit of panic", Douzi said: "Everybody was having the same feeling and trying to get out."
Some fans reported eye and respiratory symptoms, according to the North West Ambulance Service.
Hannah Baxter, who went to the concert with her partner, said the first thing she noticed was a burning feeling in her throat.
"[We] were just coughing and coughing... there was a guy next to us who had vomited. There were people with red eyes and... tears everywhere," she told the BBC.
Joey Howe, a football journalist at the gig, told BBC Radio Manchester there was a "horrible smell" and added: "People were coming through in wheelchairs choking – it was really distressing."
Police launched an investigation and are continuing to carry out tests on items at the venue to try to identify the substance. No arrests have been made.
Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "Enquiries remain ongoing to establish the nature of the substance, where it came from and any associated risk. Testing will take place throughout the day as the investigation into the cause of this incident progresses.
"We are trying to establish whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident."
Some fans complained about security and a lack of searches as people went into the Manchester concert.
Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they left the venue, adding she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".
Malachi Clarke also claimed security was "not good at all", adding: "They weren't checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine."
Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".
It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".
Figen Murray, the mother of a Manchester Arena attack victim who led the campaign for a new law to prevent terrorist attacks at public venues, said people should feel "assured" about security measures.
"A lot of the big venues use mass screening technology, where you don't even know you've been checked," she told the BBC. They also have staff observing CCTV, security guards and plain-clothed officers on site.
Murray said that while the current technology is "good enough", it needed improvement over the next few years to become "more sophisticated".
Venues are currently focused on keeping out items – such as explosives – that could cause mass casualties, she added.
Police investigate unknown substance that caused Manchester's Co-op Live evacuation
'People were screaming in pain' during Co-op Live evacuation
All fans at the Manchester show will get a full refund, promoter Live Nation said.
A statement said: "We are sorry to everyone affected by last night's events in Manchester and full refunds for that show will be automatically processed to ticket holders."
There have apparently been similar incidents earlier on Toliver's tour, when some fans reported spray or gas being released into the crowd in Zurich and Paris.
In his post on Monday, the rapper said: "I just wanna make sure everyone is safe and the next show goes on properly. My heart and prayers are with everyone that was injured last night."
"The only thing I love more than creating music is performing for my fans," Toliver said, asking people to stop bringing substances into his shows.
"It ain't cool," added the rapper, who was nominated for five Grammy Awards earlier this month. "See you soon London, love you Guys. DT."
Toliver's Nitrous tour, named after his new album, is also due to visit Wembley Arena in London on Tuesday. No update has been given about that show.
It was set to be the last gig of his world tour before he took a break from the road ahead of a Coachella appearance next spring.
Toliver is best known for singles such as No Idea and After Party, from his debut studio album, Heaven or Hell (2020), which was big on TikTok. He also featured on Travis Scott's song Can't Say, from his third studio album Astroworld.

People had warned me it might be tough to get Amish people to talk to me as a journalist — and probably impossible to get their permission to record their voice. Not a great omen for compelling radio storytelling.
Yet as I headed off to Lancaster County, Pa., last month to report on the biggest and deadliest measles outbreak in the U.S. in decades, I knew I wanted to hear directly from the community hit hardest.
So I turned to some good old shoe-leather reporting. My producer and I mapped out Amish-owned businesses in and around Lancaster County and spent a day driving around from shop to shop. At every stop, we introduced ourselves and explained the focus of our story. We asked Amish people (easily identifiable by their traditional dress) about their views on the measles outbreak and vaccination. While some declined to talk, others opened up about how measles had affected their families and communities, and why they had or hadn't decided to get vaccinated. To my surprise, one woman even let me record her voice.
Outside a farm supply store in a rural town, I met an Amish woman who was visibly pregnant. Measles can have devastating consequences during pregnancy. She told me her husband and two children had gotten vaccinated to protect her and her unborn child. She declined to give me her name at first, then got in a car driven by her hired non-Amish driver. As they exited the parking lot, the driver stopped to ask us what media outlet we were with. "Oh, NPR!" the driver said when we replied. Then she turned to her Amish passenger and told her, "Don't worry, you can trust them."
Part of gaining trust is about showing up, showing respect and really listening. Word gets around that you're trustworthy. Public health officials in Pennsylvania have also been using a similar approach to win the trust of Amish people as they seek to boost vaccination rates in the current outbreak. You can read more about it here .

Almanya ve Danimarka genelindeki yüzlerce okula pazartesi sabahı e-posta yoluyla bomba tehdidi gönderildi. Almanya'da 450 okulun tehdit e-postalarından etkilendiği duyuruldu. Polis birimleri olayla ilgili geniş çaplı bir inceleme başlattı. Yetkililer, iletişime geçilen okullarda somut bir tehdide rastlanmadığını bildirdi.
Almanya 'nın güneybatısındaki Freiburg kentinden polis yetkilileri, ülke genelinde 450 okulun tehdit e-postalarından etkilendiğini duyurdu. Açıklamada okulların durumuna ilişkin şu ifadeler kullanıldı:
'Şu an itibarıyla iletişime geçilen okulların somut bir tehditle karşı karşıya olduğuna dair herhangi bir kanıt bulunmamaktadır.'
Polis, e-postaların gönderildiği okullarla temas kurmayı sürdürüyor.
Berlin polisi de Freiburg'dakine benzer bir değerlendirme yaptı. Thüringen eyalet polisi ise okullara eğitime normal şekilde devam etmeleri yönünde bilgi verildiğini açıkladı. Yetkililer, faillerin asıl amacının eyleme geçmekten çok panik ve korku yaratmak olduğunu değerlendiriyor. Bu yüzden derslerin aksatılmaması istendi.
Danimarka polisi, ülke genelindeki çeşitli okullara yönelik bomba tehditlerini soruşturduğunu bildirdi. Danimarkalı yetkililer de mevcut aşamada endişe edilecek bir durum bulunmadığını vurguladı. Avrupa'da son dönemde okulları, süpermarketleri, kan bankalarını, hava trafik sistemlerini ve yayın kuruluşlarını hedef alan asılsız ihbarlar ve siber saldırılar günlük yaşamı aksatıyor. Geçen hafta İspanya 'da 10'dan fazla okul , e-posta yoluyla gelen bomba tehditleri yüzünden tahliye edildi. Bu ayın başlarında İtalya 'da binlerce okula benzer e-postalar gönderilmiş, tahliye kararları alınmıştı. Birleşik Krallık'ta da aynı gün çeşitli ihbarlar yapıldı.

Avrupa genelindeki okullara son haftalarda gönderilen sahte bomba ihbarlarının ardından Almanya'daki bazı okullara da bomba tehdidi içeren e-postalar gönderildi. Polis, pazartesi günü yaptığı açıklamada şu aşamada “somut bir tehlike” bulunmadığını bildirdi.
Polisin açıklamasına göre, ülkenin güneybatısındaki Baden-Württemberg eyaletinde 450'den fazla okul tehdit içeren e-postalar aldı.
Doğudaki Thüringen eyaletinde de çok sayıda okula bomba tehdidi gönderildiğini belirten polis, ihbarların gerçek olduğunun düşünülmediğini açıkladı.
Danimarka polisi de ülke genelinde bazı okullara gönderilen bomba tehditleriyle ilgili soruşturma yürütüldüğünü ancak endişe duyulmasını gerektiren bir durum bulunmadığını bildirdi.
Bu gelişmeler, İtalya'da ay başında 300'den fazla okulun e-postayla gönderilen bomba tehditleri nedeniyle tahliye edilmesinin ardından geldi. Söz konusu e-postalarda, Başbakan Giorgia Meloni'nin aracına da patlayıcı yerleştirildiği iddia edilmişti.
Meloni, Facebook hesabından yaptığı paylaşımda, “Şu ana kadar gerçekleştirilen kontrollerde somut bir tehlike bulunduğuna işaret eden herhangi bir unsur ortaya çıkmadı,” dedi.
Eğitim Bakanı Giuseppe Valditara, ülke genelinde yaklaşık 300 ihbar kaydedildiğini belirterek, “Açıkça bir strateji söz konusu,” dedi.
E-postalar, “Sizi yok etmeye geldik. İtalyanlara karşı soykırım gerçekleştireceğiz,” ifadeleriyle başlıyordu. Mesajlarda her okul binasına uzaktan kumandayla patlatılabilen “güçlü bir patlayıcı düzenek” yerleştirildiği öne sürülüyordu.
E-postalarda ayrıca, “Başbakanınızın arabasının motoruna bomba yerleştirdik,” deniliyordu. Mesajlar, kendisini “Misojinistan Vilayeti lideri Mihail Andropov” olarak tanıtan bir kişi tarafından imzalanmıştı.
Geçen hafta İrlanda ve Bulgaristan'daki medya kuruluşlarına gönderilen bomba tehditleri de aynı isimle imzalanmıştı.
Benzer sahte tehditler 11 Kasım'da İngiltere ve İrlanda'daki okullarda da bildirilmiş, bazı okullar tahliye edilmişti.
Bu olaydan yaklaşık bir hafta sonra İtalya'da en az 100 okul daha e-posta ve zehir tehdidi almış, bunun üzerine hükümet yeni bir güvenlik protokolünü devreye sokmuştu.
İtalya Dışişleri Bakanı Antonio Tajani, Brüksel'de yaptığı açıklamada, “E-posta, siber saldırı veya korsanlık yoluyla gerçekleştirilen farklı türdeki saldırılara karşılık verme ve tehditleri önleme konusunda giderek daha fazla birlik olma yönünde ortak bir görüş ve irade var,” dedi.

King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.
Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.
Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars, with the king on Monday calling him "a true giant of the music industry".
Born in Victoria in 1943, Meldrum displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.
Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.
Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.
"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," a statement from Meldrum's family said.
Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.
He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".
King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special , saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".
On Monday, an aide to the King said he had been "deeply saddened" to hear of Meldrum's death.
"His Majesty's interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget - he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honour Molly's legacy as a true giant of the music industry."
Elton John - a friend and regular interviewee - paid tribute to him as "an Australian legend and an institution", while pop star Kylie Minogue said she would be turning up the music in his honour.
"As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room."
"He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I'm so grateful for his unwavering love and support."
Australia's Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon: "One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music."

LEGO, Avrupa, Orta Doğu ve Afrika genelinde artan talebi karşılamak için Portekiz'in Estarreja kentinde yeni bir fabrika için yaklaşık 1 milyar euro yatırım yapma planını pazartesi günü açıkladı.
LEGO, fabrikanın tam kapasiteyle faaliyete geçtiğinde 1.000'den fazla kişiyi istihdam edeceğini, burada nitelikli üretim işleri sunulacağını ve üretimin 2030'da başlamasının beklendiğini bildirdi.
LEGO'nun üst yöneticisi Niels B. Christiansen, "Estarreja'daki yeni fabrikamızı duyurmaktan büyük heyecan duyuyoruz. Küresel üretim ağımızı genişletmemiz, büyümeye devam etmek ve LEGO oyununu gelecek nesiller boyunca çok daha fazla çocuğa, aileye ve hayrana ulaştırmak için güçlü bir konumda kalacağımız anlamına geliyor," dedi.
Tesis, Danimarka, Macaristan ve Çekya'daki fabrikalarına ek olarak LEGO'nun Avrupa'daki dördüncü fabrikası olacak.
LEGO'nun operasyonlardan sorumlu üst yöneticisi Carsten Rasmussen, "Pazarlara yakınlığı, ulaşım bağlantılarına erişimi, sürdürülebilirliğe bağlılığı ve yetenekli yerel işgücü sayesinde Portekiz bizim için öne çıktı," dedi.
115 bin metrekarelik fabrika, yaklaşık 60 hektarlık bir alan üzerinde, aşağı yukarı 120 futbol sahası büyüklüğünde kurulacak. İnşaat alanı bakımından Macaristan'daki Nyíregyháza fabrikasının yarısından daha küçük olacak. Yeni tesiste LEGO parçaları kalıplanıp işlenecek ve hazır setler paketlenecek.
Rasmussen, burasının LEGO'nun en otomatikleştirilmiş fabrikası olacağını söyledi. Rasmussen, "Bu yeni fabrika, üretkenliği, sürdürülebilirliği ve operasyonel dayanıklılığı artırmak için yenilikçi teknolojilerin kullanılacağı en otomatik ve en gelişmiş tesisimiz olacak," dedi.
Portekiz Başbakanı Luís Montenegro, pazartesi günü Estarreja'daki tanıtım törenine katıldı. Hükümetin, arazinin tahsisini sağlamak ve inşaatı hızlandırmak için çalışacağını, böylece istihdamın mümkün olan en kısa sürede yaratılabileceğini söyledi.
İnşaatın 2027'nin ilk yarısında başlaması bekleniyor. Portekiz'deki tesis, 2027'de açılması planlanan Virginia fabrikasının ardından LEGO'nun dünya genelindeki sekizinci fabrikası olacak. LEGO, ürünlerini müşterilere daha yakın yerlerde üretmenin tedarik zincirlerini kısaltacağını ve taşımacılığın çevresel etkisini azaltacağını belirtiyor.
LEGO, Estarreja fabrikasının yıllık enerji ihtiyacının tamamını yenilenebilir kaynaklardan karşılamayı hedefliyor. Şirket, güneş panelleri ve batarya depolama sistemleri de dahil olmak üzere sahadaki altyapının bu ihtiyacın yaklaşık yüzde 80'ini karşılamasını bekliyor.
LEGO'nun tüketici satışları 2026'nın ilk yarısında yüzde 22 yükseldi. Gelir yüzde 21 artarak 41,9 milyar Danimarka kronuna (5,6 milyar euro) çıkarken, faaliyet kârı yüzde 22 artışla 10,9 milyar DKK'ya (1,5 milyar euro) ulaştı. Şirket, gelir artışına katkıda bulunan bölgeler arasında Batı Avrupa'yı özellikle öne çıkardı.
LEGO, 2025'te Macaristan'daki fabrikasında üretim kapasitesini yüzde 30 artırdı ve Haziran 2026'da Danimarka'nın Billund kentinde bir üretim inovasyon merkezi açtı. Şirket ayrıca Çin'deki fabrikasını genişletti ve eylülde Meksika'nın Monterrey kentindeki tesisinde kapasite artışına gitme planlarını duyurdu.
Şirket, Nisan 2025'te Vietnam'da bir fabrika açtı ve 2027'de Virginia'da hem bir fabrika hem de bölgesel bir dağıtım merkezi açmayı bekliyor.
